extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and aesthetics; readers of Kant's Critique of Judgement
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for making and evaluating aesthetic (taste) judgements in Kant's Critique of Judgement: how beauty, purposiveness, pleasure, and disinterestedness ground judgements of taste and their claimed (subjective) universality. Focuses on the distinction between aesthetic and teleological judgement and on the threefold contrast of pleasant/good/beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste is aesthetical
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste is aesthetical: to decide whether anything is beautiful we refer the representation not to the Understanding for cognition but to the subject (Imagination, perhaps with Understanding) and its feeling of pleasure or pain; its determining ground can be only subjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the difference between objective reference (representation referred to the object for cognition) and aesthetical reference (referred to the subject and feeling). Example contrast: apprehending a regular, purposive building cognitively vs being conscious of satisfaction. Aesthetic judgement adds nothing to cognition; it compares a given representation in the subject with the whole faculty of representations (the subject's state).

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction determining judgement of taste must be disinterested
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction that determines a judgement of taste is disinterested: when judging beauty we must be indifferent to the existence of the object (no interest in its possession, utility, or existence), so the judgement is 'pure' and not mixed with other interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by examples (palace admired by different motives, Rousseau's critique, hypothetical island). Any judgement where the least interest mingles is partial and not a pure judgement of taste. The critic must not be prejudiced in favour of the object's existence to be a proper judge of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasantness is bound up with interest (sensory)
rubrics_metrics.description: What pleases the senses in sensation is 'pleasant'; this pleasure is tied to interest because it excites desire and relates to the existence or possession of the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes objective sensation (perceptual content like green meadows) from subjective sensation (feeling, which arouses inclination). Pleasantness gratifies and presupposes relation of the object's existence to the subject's state. Those who seek only enjoyment are not making judgments of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good (moral/intellectual) is bound up with interest via concept
rubrics_metrics.description: That which pleases through the mere concept (to Reason) is 'good'; 'good for something' (useful) vs 'good in itself' involves a concept of purpose and relation to will, and thus interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To call something good requires a concept of what it ought to be (hence reflection by Reason). Contrasts with beautiful: the beautiful can please without any concept, whereas the good presupposes conceptual determination and often ties to volition or utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful arises from disinterested pleasure in form (subjective purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: An object is judged beautiful when its form, apprehended without reference to a concept for cognition, immediately arouses a feeling of pleasure; this pleasure signals a subjective formal purposiveness of the object (harmony of Imagination and Understanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pleasure in beauty is not a sensation tied to desire nor a concept-based approval; it is felt in mere reflection upon form and is the ground of taste. Flowers and free delineations (foliage) please without depending on concepts. The judgment of beauty claims universal validity because its ground is the 'universal though only subjective' condition of reflective judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: subjective (aesthetical) vs objective (teleological) purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Purposiveness may be represented subjectively as harmony of form with cognitive faculties (aesthetic) or objectively as harmony of form with the concept of the thing itself (teleological); the former is judged by Taste, the latter by Understanding and Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjective purposiveness is tied to pleasurable reflection and does not determine cognition; objective purposiveness (natural purpose) presupposes a concept of the object's end and is judged teleologically. The Critique divides into aesthetical and teleological judgement accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgement claims universal validity despite its empirical ground
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the judgement of taste is an empirical feeling (not a concept), it nevertheless claims validity for everyone because the ground of the pleasure lies in the universal (though subjective) conditions of reflective judgement—the purposive harmony of cognitive faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: a singular empirical judgement of experience can claim universality when formed under laws of possible experience; similarly, the feeling-based judgement of taste claims agreement of everyone because its ground is the common structure of reflective judgement (Imagination with Understanding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgement is not a cognitive/determinant judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic judgements do not determine objects for cognition (they do not supply concepts); they are reflective and judge by feeling, not by providing determinative principles for understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic judgement compares representations with the subject's faculties and contributes nothing to the knowledge of objects; it is a critique of the judging subject and its faculties insofar as they are susceptible of a priori principles of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness of nature as principle for reflection (regulative, not constitutive)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Judgement presupposes a principle a priori of nature's specification for our cognitive faculty—an ideal purposiveness that guides reflection but does not prescribe objective laws to nature; it is regulative, allowing investigation to proceed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presupposition is subjective and indeterminate in extent; it permits the Understanding to seek unity of principles in nature's diversity but does not establish objective determinative rules about when to apply purposive judgement rather than natural laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure from discovery of unity (comprehensibility) grounds aesthetic pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: A marked pleasure (often admiration) arises when heterogeneous empirical laws of nature are found to be combinable under a single comprehending principle; this discovery of unity contributes to pleasure distinct from mere cognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such pleasure can become habitual and indistinguishable from cognition with familiarity, but originally it alerts us to purposiveness of nature for our understanding. Conversely, representation of irreducible heterogeneity would displease, as it frustrates reflective judgement's aim to find unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste requires comparison of Imagination and Understanding (harmony) in reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste rests on the harmony (unity) between Imagination (a priori form of intuition) and Understanding (concepts) in the subject during reflection; this harmony is the basis for calling something purposive and beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The form of the object for reflection, when purposive for cognitive faculties without reference to concept or desire, produces disinterested pleasure. This 'play' of faculties is spontaneous and the source of the feeling that grounds taste and its claimed universality.
